3. 'Your connections' tab: record every connection, its source and its state
4. Select a connection: the details pane shows the 'Permissions' section
5. Check that the selected mode is 'Only people with access to this data source' and not 'Visible to everyone'
6. For any connection set to 'Visible to everyone': obtain a written justification approved by the CISO, or delete the connection and re-create it with the restricted mode, since that mode cannot be changed after creation
7. Have the security team approve the legitimacy of each source and the audience of its content, and record the decision in the approval register
8. Run this control again before every new connection goes live, as the decision can no longer be reversed afterwards
items.Expected: Every Microsoft Graph connector connection indexes its content while honouring the source permissions ('Only people with access to this data source'). Any connection set to 'Visible to everyone' is justified in writing, limited to content that is explicitly public internally, and approved by the CISO. No active connection is missing from the security team approval register.
items.Verification: GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/external/connections?$select=id,name,description,state,configuration (ExternalConnection.Read.All scope) for the inventory, then GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/external/connections/{id}/groups for the permission indicator: a connection that projects its source permissions declares external groups, a connection set to 'Visible to everyone' declares none. Since the permission mode itself is exposed by no documented property of externalConnection, confirmation is done in admin.cloud.microsoft > Copilot > Connectors > Your connections > details pane > Permissions.

items.Requirement: Enable auditing of interactions with Copilot agents
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Click the 'Audit' card (or left-hand menu: Audit)
3. Click 'New search'
4. In the 'Activities' field: search for and select 'Copilot activities' > 'Interacted with Copilot'
5. Set the date range
6. Optional: filter by user
7. Run the search
--- Note ---
The technical record type is 'CopilotInteraction'
items.Expected: Copilot interactions present in the audit log over a rolling 7-day window with at least one identified agent (non-empty AgentId); the ConnectedAIAppInteraction and AIAppInteraction record types enabled where third-party AI applications are deployed; no record carrying XPIADetected=true or JailbreakDetected=true (target: 0, otherwise investigate)
items.Verification: Search-UnifiedAuditLog -RecordType CopilotInteraction -StartDate (Get-Date).AddDays(-7) -EndDate (Get-Date) -ResultSize 500 | ForEach-Object { $_.AuditData | ConvertFrom-Json } | Select-Object AgentId, AgentName, AppIdentity, AppHost, XPIADetected ; then Search-UnifiedAuditLog -RecordType ConnectedAIAppInteraction and -RecordType AIAppInteraction
items.Rationale: Every interaction with a Copilot agent must be traceable in order to meet regulatory compliance requirements and to support security investigations. Simply checking that CopilotInteraction records exist is no longer sufficient. First, these records now carry the AgentId, AgentName and AgentVersion properties: traceability must be verified PER AGENT, otherwise an entire agent can be missing from the logs without anyone noticing. Second, interactions with third-party AI applications are logged under the ConnectedAIAppInteraction and AIAppInteraction record types, which are billed on a Microsoft Purview pay-as-you-go basis and are NOT enabled by default: without that activation, those interactions appear nowhere. Third, the record exposes XPIADetected, a boolean that flags an indirect prompt injection attempt through a document that was accessed, together with Messages.JailbreakDetected. Failing to use these fields deprives the organisation of the only signal available on attacks targeting its agents, and makes any investigation impossible after a data leak through an agent.

items.Requirement: Establish a naming convention for agents and measure how far it is followed
items.Rationale: Without a naming convention, Copilot agents pile up under vague or duplicate names (for example 'My HR agent', 'Recruitment agent', 'HR Bot') that make it impossible to identify their purpose, their owner and the data they reach. A structured nomenclature such as Department-Function-Agent eases administration, security review and discovery by users. A convention is only worth anything, however, once compliance with it is measured: the agent registry exposes the displayName of every package, which makes it possible to compare each organisation-authored agent against the agreed pattern automatically and to obtain a compliance rate rather than an intention. The convention belongs to the customer: the engine only assesses names when the pattern is supplied to it, and otherwise inventories the observed names without raising any gap.
items.HowTo:
1. Define a convention: [Department]-[Function]-Agent
   Examples: HR-Recruitment-Agent, Finance-Budget-Agent, IT-Support-Agent
2. Translate it into a regular expression, for example ^(HR|Finance|IT)-[A-Za-z0-9]+-Agent$
3. Document the convention in the Copilot usage policy and communicate it to agent authors
4. Re-run the engine with -AgentNamingPattern '<regular expression>' to measure the compliance rate
5. Rename non-compliant agents from their administration page
--- Note ---
The expression is applied as supplied, with no implicit anchoring: add ^ and $ to require a full match, (?i) to ignore case. Only agents whose publisher is not Microsoft are assessed
items.Expected: Convention documented, communicated and supplied to the engine through -AgentNamingPattern; 100% of agents created inside the organisation match the pattern
items.Verification: GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/copilot/admin/catalog/packages (CopilotPackages.Read.All scope, Microsoft Agent 365 licence), then compare displayName against the pattern passed to -AgentNamingPattern, excluding Microsoft-published agents

items.Requirement: Create an approval process for new agents
items.Rationale: Each Copilot agent inherits the permissions of the user who runs it and can therefore reach every email, file and conversation that user is able to read. An agent created without validation may contain instructions that skew its answers, reach sensitive data sources or generate inappropriate content. An approval process (creation, IT validation, testing, publication) guarantees that every agent is reviewed for its security, its relevance and its compliance before being deployed. Without this process, the organisation has no control over the agents that access its data and interact with its employees.
items.HowTo:
1. Define the process: creation > IT validation > testing > publication
2. Create a request form (Forms or a SharePoint list)
3. Required fields: name, purpose, data accessed, target audience
4. Appoint approvers (IT or security team)
5. Document it in the Copilot governance policy
--- Note ---
There is no native approval workflow in the portal -- it must be set up manually or through Power Automate
items.Expected: Approval process documented and operational
items.Verification: Manual check of the process

items.Requirement: Document a usage policy for Copilot agents
items.Rationale: A usage policy for Copilot agents is the equivalent of a Teams usage charter or an IT security policy: it sets the rules of the game for every user. It must state who is authorised to create agents, which data sources are forbidden (medical data, social insurance numbers, salary information), which use cases are prohibited and what the user's responsibility is for the answers generated. Without this policy documented and communicated, every user invents their own rules, which creates compliance risks and inconsistencies in the way agents are used across the organisation.
items.HowTo:
1. Write a document covering:
   - Who is authorised to create agents
   - Approval process
   - Naming convention
   - Data forbidden in agents (social insurance numbers, medical information, etc.)
   - User responsibility for the answers
2. Publish it on the Copilot resources SharePoint site
3. Have it signed off / acknowledged by the authorised users
items.Expected: Usage policy documented, published and communicated
items.Verification: Manual check of the document

items.Requirement: Periodic review of deployed agents (quarterly), backed by the agent registry
items.Rationale: The quarterly review of agents is currently documented as a manual ritual, which makes it unverifiable and therefore rarely carried out. Microsoft now exposes the full inventory of tenant agents in Microsoft Graph, through the Copilot package management API (the Microsoft Agent 365 agent registry). The engine can enumerate every agent together with its publisher, its supported hosts, its publication scope, its blocked state and its last-modified date. Without that automated inventory, the organisation has no idea how many agents are really active, and abandoned agents (test agents never deleted, agents built for a finished project, agents whose owner has left the organisation) keep reaching Microsoft 365 data. The exposed date is a last-modified date and not a usage date: an agent unchanged for more than 90 days is a candidate for review rather than a gap in itself, and the decision is cross-checked against the Copilot usage report. Access to this API requires the Microsoft Agent 365 licence together with the AI Administrator or Global Administrator role: without them the check is not applicable rather than failed.
items.HowTo:
1. The engine queries the agent registry: GET /v1.0/copilot/admin/catalog/packages
2. It reports the number of agents, the split by publisher, the blocked agents and the agents unchanged for more than 90 days
3. For each flagged agent: identify the owner, cross-check with the Copilot usage report, verify the data sources it reaches
4. Block or delete agents with no confirmed usage from admin.cloud.microsoft > Copilot > Agents
5. Validate that retained agents comply with the usage policy
6. Document the review outcome and the date of the next one
--- Note ---
The check requires the Microsoft Agent 365 licence and the AI Administrator (or Global Administrator) role; without the licence it reports as not applicable and leaves the compliance rate
items.Expected: Inventory retrieved successfully (HTTP 200); every agent carries an identified publisher; no agent unchanged for more than 90 days without a recorded review decision; no agent unknown to the last governance review
items.Verification: GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/copilot/admin/catalog/packages?$filter=supportedHosts/any(h:h eq 'Copilot') (CopilotPackages.Read.All scope, AI Administrator or Global Administrator role, Microsoft Agent 365 licence), then analysis of publisher, isBlocked and lastModifiedDateTime

items.Requirement: Configure sensitivity labels (minimum three levels) and grant the VIEW and EXTRACT usage rights to the Copilot populations
items.Rationale: Sensitivity labels are the bedrock of data protection in a Copilot environment: they classify documents and attach automatic protections to them, encryption included. Counting them is not enough, because the most common and the most silent misconfiguration of a Copilot deployment lies in the usage rights defined on those labels. Microsoft documents that an AI application only returns the content of an encrypted item when the calling identity holds not just the VIEW right but also the EXTRACT (copy) right. A 'Confidential' label configured with VIEW and EDIT but without EXTRACT, the natural reflex when the goal was to prevent copy and paste, makes every document carrying it invisible to Copilot. The failure is entirely silent: no error message, the documents simply never appear in answers, and the team concludes there is an indexing defect or a service regression. The same effect occurs with labels using user-defined permissions, which Copilot cannot open outside SharePoint and OneDrive. The discovery comes after go-live, on precisely the corpus that justified the project, while the requirement was reported as compliant. The check therefore inspects the rights definition of every encrypting label, identity by identity, rather than the mere existence of the labels.
items.Expected: >= 3 active labels with an increasing protection hierarchy; for every label with EncryptionEnabled = True protected by a template, EncryptionRightsDefinitions grants VIEW and EXTRACT (or OWNER, which implicitly carries both) to the identities that must benefit from Copilot. An encrypting label granting EXTRACT to no identity is a gap: its content is invisible to Copilot. Raised as warnings: identities deprived of EXTRACT on an otherwise correct label, labels using user-defined permissions, unreadable rights definitions, and a hierarchy containing no encrypting label at all.
items.Verification: Get-Label | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, Priority, Disabled, EncryptionEnabled, EncryptionProtectionType, EncryptionRightsDefinitions
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Left-hand menu: Solutions > Information Protection > Sensitivity labels
3. Check that at least 3 active, tiered labels exist (Public, Internal, Confidential, Highly confidential)
4. Open each label that applies encryption > Edit > Encryption
5. Choose 'Assign permissions now' (user-defined permissions prevent Copilot from opening the item outside SharePoint and OneDrive)
6. For each target group or domain: pick a permission level that includes View (VIEW) and Copy (EXTRACT), or define custom permissions containing both rights
7. Save, republish the label policy, then check: Get-Label | Select-Object DisplayName, EncryptionEnabled, EncryptionProtectionType, EncryptionRightsDefinitions
8. Confirm on a test document that Copilot does cite a file carrying the encrypting label

items.Requirement: Publish the sensitivity labels to Copilot users
items.Rationale: Creating sensitivity labels in Purview is not enough: they must be published to users through a publishing policy in order to appear in the Office applications and be usable. Without publication, the labels exist in the admin portal but are completely invisible to users, which makes the whole classification configuration pointless. The publishing policy also makes it possible to set a default label (recommended: 'Internal') that is applied automatically to every new document, preventing files from being left unclassified. Without this step, no document is classified and Copilot cannot tell the sensitivity levels apart.
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Solutions > Information Protection
3. Click 'Publishing policies'
4. Click 'Publish label'
5. Select all the labels created
6. Publish to: the GRP-Copilot-Users group
7. Default label for documents: 'Internal' (recommended)
8. Mandatory label for emails: Yes (recommended)
9. Create the policy
items.Expected: Active publishing policy targeting the Copilot group
items.Verification: Get-LabelPolicy | Select Name, Labels

items.Requirement: Enable auto-labelling for new files
items.Rationale: Auto-labelling automatically analyses the content of files and emails to detect sensitive information (social insurance numbers, credit card numbers, medical data) and applies the appropriate sensitivity label with no human intervention. This automation is essential, because manual classification is rarely applied consistently by users. In a Copilot environment, an unclassified file containing personal data can be cited in the Copilot answers of unauthorised users. Without auto-labelling, the majority of existing files remain unclassified and Copilot handles them with no additional protection whatsoever.
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Solutions > Information Protection
3. Policies > Auto-labeling policies
4. Create a policy > Name: 'AutoLabel-SensitiveData'
5. Conditions: detect the sensitive information types (SIN, credit card, NIN)
6. Action: apply the 'Confidential' label
7. Locations: SharePoint + OneDrive + Exchange
8. Mode: simulation first (30 days), then activation
items.Expected: At least 1 auto-labelling policy active or in simulation
items.Verification: Get-AutoSensitivityLabelPolicy | Select Name, Mode

items.Requirement: Configure DLP policies covering the four workloads and the Microsoft 365 Copilot location
items.Rationale: DLP policies watch the flow of sensitive data across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams, and block or alert when protected information is shared inappropriately. Those four locations nevertheless leave the AI surface entirely uncovered: they govern what the user shares, never what Copilot consumes to build an answer. Microsoft Purview now exposes a fifth policy location, 'Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Chat', which prevents Copilot from using the content of a file or an email carrying a given label when generating a response. It is the only mechanism that separates the user's right of access from the AI's right of exploitation: the item stays accessible and may appear as a citation, but its content is neither read nor summarised. Without this policy, a document labelled 'Highly confidential' whose permissions are too broad is summarised word for word on the very first prompt, which historical oversharing makes statistically certain on any tenant of significant size. It is the last-line control for as long as permission remediation is unfinished, and it deploys in hours where remediation takes months. A policy left in simulation withholds no content, and a policy without a rule applying RestrictAccess / ExcludeContentProcessing prevents nothing: both cases are reported distinctly. Changes take up to four hours to be honoured by the service.
items.Expected: >= 1 active DLP policy (Mode = Enable, not TestWithNotifications or TestWithoutNotifications) covering the Microsoft 365 Copilot location (CopilotExperiences enforcement plane or location 470f2276-e011-4e9d-a6ec-20768be3a4b0), with at least one rule applying the RestrictAccess / ExcludeContentProcessing action, preferably on the 'Content contains > Sensitivity labels' condition and on the top-tier labels. The four historical workloads (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams) remain required: the Copilot location adds to them, it does not replace them.
items.Verification: Get-DlpCompliancePolicy | Select-Object Name, Mode, Enabled, Workload, EnforcementPlanes, Locations ; Get-DlpComplianceRule | Select-Object Name, ParentPolicyName, Disabled, RestrictAccess, AdvancedRule
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Left-hand menu: Data Loss Prevention > Policies > Create policy
3. Choose 'Custom' and name the policy (for example DLP-Copilot-Grounding)
4. Locations: tick 'Microsoft 365 Copilot' in addition to Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams
5. Rule: condition 'Content contains' > 'Sensitivity labels' > select the top-tier labels (Highly confidential, Confidential)
6. Action: prevent Copilot from processing the content (RestrictAccess / ExcludeContentProcessing)
7. Mode: start in simulation, then switch to 'Turn it on' - in simulation no content is withheld from Copilot
8. Create the policy and allow up to 4 hours before checking again
9. Verify: Get-DlpCompliancePolicy | Where-Object { $_.Mode -eq 'Enable' } | Select-Object Name, Workload, EnforcementPlanes

items.Requirement: Configure retention for Copilot interactions on the Purview AI locations
items.Rationale: The requirement is functionally sound but technically out of date: Microsoft has separated Copilot retention from the former 'Teams chats and Copilot interactions' location and split it into three distinct locations (Microsoft 365 Copilot experiences, Enterprise AI apps, Other AI apps). These new locations are NOT managed by Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy, but by the Get-AppRetentionCompliancePolicy / Get-AppRetentionComplianceRule family. The practical consequence: a check based on the former cmdlet systematically returns zero results on a correctly configured tenant, producing a permanent false negative on a compliance requirement. Conversely, a tenant that only holds an old 'Teams chats and Copilot interactions' policy no longer covers recent Copilot Chat interactions. Every Copilot interaction (the prompt and the generated response) remains business data subject to the same legal retention obligations as emails or documents: both cmdlet families must therefore be checked, and the User:M365Copilot application must be required explicitly.
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Left-hand menu: Solutions > Data Lifecycle Management
3. Policies > Retention policies > New policy

items.Rationale: The 90-day threshold is out of date: since 17 October 2023, the default retention of Audit (Standard) has been 180 days, no longer 90. A check that passes at 90 days therefore declares compliant a tenant that has in fact configured nothing, which empties the requirement of its substance. In addition, AI-related logs are now spread across several record types: CopilotInteraction (Microsoft Copilot), ConnectedAIAppInteraction (Copilot Studio agents and AI applications registered in the tenant) and AIAppInteraction (third-party AI applications, billed on a pay-as-you-go basis, retained for 180 days). An audit retention policy that does not cover these types leaves the organisation without usable evidence beyond the default window in the event of a dispute or a regulatory review of AI usage.

2. Left-hand menu: Audit

items.Requirement: Verify eDiscovery on Copilot data: API accessibility, named managers and interaction search
items.Rationale: The requirement was classified as 'manual' even though a stable Microsoft Graph v1.0 API now exists for eDiscovery: GET /security/cases/ediscoveryCases lists cases read-only with the eDiscovery.Read.All permission (or the eDiscovery Manager role when running delegated). That single call is doubly informative: a 200 proves that the tenant holds an active eDiscovery (Premium) licence and that the audit account genuinely holds the right, whereas a 403 states precisely which of the two is missing. It also reveals whether the organisation has instrumented eDiscovery or whether the capability has never been exercised. Complemented on the Purview side by the equally read-only reading of the 'eDiscovery Manager' role group members and of the compliance searches that target Copilot interactions, it turns a declarative verification into an objective finding. Without this instrumentation, the organisation discovers at the moment of a legal order that it can neither preserve nor produce Copilot prompts and responses, even though these are stored in a hidden mailbox folder and remain perfectly searchable through the ItemClass IPM.SkypeTeams.Message.Copilot.* condition or the Type > Copilot activity filter.
items.Expected: GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/security/cases/ediscoveryCases returns 200 (evidence of the eDiscovery (Premium) licence and of the effective permission), the 'eDiscovery Manager' role group has at least one named member, and at least one eDiscovery case or one compliance search targeting Copilot interactions exists on the tenant. A 403 with no eDiscovery (Premium) service plan detected makes the requirement not applicable; a 403 with the licence present indicates that the audit account lacks the rights. The engine creates no case, no search and no export: the probe is strictly read-only.
items.Verification: GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/security/cases/ediscoveryCases ; Connect-IPPSSession then Get-RoleGroupMember -Identity 'eDiscovery Manager' ; Get-ComplianceSearch | Select-Object Name, Status, ContentMatchQuery
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://purview.microsoft.com
2. Settings > Roles and scopes > Role groups: check that the 'eDiscovery Manager' group has at least one named member
3. Solutions > eDiscovery: create a test case on a pilot user
4. In the case: add a search with the ItemClass IPM.SkypeTeams.Message.Copilot.* condition (or the Type > Copilot activity filter)
5. Check that the results contain the Copilot prompts and responses, then validate the export
6. On the permissions side: grant eDiscovery.Read.All (application) or the eDiscovery Manager / eDiscovery Administrator role (delegated) to the audit account
7. Check the API: GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/security/cases/ediscoveryCases must return 200

items.Requirement: Generate and track the SharePoint data access governance reports
items.Rationale: The data access governance (DAG) reports detail overshared sites, content reachable by an excessive number of users and active sharing links. They were marked Manual and Optimal, which was wrong on both counts: a complete PowerShell API has existed since Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell 16.0.25409. Start-SPODataAccessGovernanceInsight triggers the reports, Get-SPODataAccessGovernanceInsight returns their status and metadata, Export-SPODataAccessGovernanceInsight downloads the CSV. The engine, being read-only, therefore establishes whether the reports exist, whether they are Completed, how many sites they list and when they were generated; it never triggers their generation, which is a change action. The Microsoft blueprint places the permissions baseline report (PermissionedUsers) as the first action before any Copilot deployment, because it is the only way to know how many users are actually permissioned on each site before Copilot makes that oversharing exploitable through natural language. Without this baseline the organisation deploys Copilot without measuring its exposure, and requirement 18 loses its data source.

At least one recent activity report with status Completed (SharingLinks_Anyone, SharingLinks_PeopleInYourOrg or EveryoneExceptExternalUsersAtSite). Failing an activity report, audit data collection must be InProgress.

4. Run an activity report: 'Sharing links' or

--- Or with PowerShell ---

7. Start-SPODataAccessGovernanceInsight -ReportEntity PermissionedUsers -Workload OneDriveForBusiness -ReportType Snapshot
8. Track progress:

items.Requirement: Enable sensitivity labels for Office files in SharePoint and OneDrive
items.Rationale: This is the missing prerequisite that silently defeats every other requirement about sensitivity labels. As long as EnableAIPIntegration stays False at SharePoint tenant level, SharePoint and OneDrive cannot process the content of Office files encrypted by a label: auto-labeling does not apply, search does not index their content, and Microsoft documents that the only encrypted files Copilot and agents can reach are then the data in use inside the Office apps on Windows. In practice, an organisation that published three levels of labels with encryption but missed this switch finds that Copilot simply ignores its protected documents, and wrongly concludes that Copilot does not work, or worse, that the documents are not protected at all. The gap is invisible from the Purview portal, which will show labels published and applied: nothing there indicates that SharePoint cannot read them. The setting is opt-in and was never on by default on tenants created before it shipped, and it is not instantly retroactive: files already encrypted are only processed after activation. In a Multi-Geo tenant the value is per geography, so a tenant can be compliant in its main geography and blind in the others. The companion setting EnableSensitivityLabelforOneNote extends the same processing to notebooks, which are otherwise left out.
items.Expected: EnableAIPIntegration = True. Recommended companion setting: EnableSensitivityLabelforOneNote = True. In a Multi-Geo tenant the value is checked and true for every geography. Leaving it off is not a target posture: it makes the labelled corpus invisible to Copilot.
items.Verification: Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object EnableAIPIntegration, EnableSensitivityLabelforOneNote
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://admin.cloud.microsoft > Admin centers > SharePoint
   (or https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com)
2. Check that sensitivity labels are published in
   https://purview.microsoft.com > Information Protection > Labels
--- Reading the state, in PowerShell ---
3. Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com
4. Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object EnableAIPIntegration, EnableSensitivityLabelforOneNote
--- Turning it on ---
5. Set-SPOTenant -EnableAIPIntegration $true
6. Set-SPOTenant -EnableSensitivityLabelforOneNote $true
7. Allow time for already encrypted files to be processed before concluding
8. Replay a Copilot query against a known labelled reference document
--- Multi-Geo ---
9. Repeat steps 3 to 6 after Connect-SPOService against each geo admin centre
--- Note ---
Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell module, SharePoint Administrator role.
The setting changes no permission: it allows SharePoint and OneDrive to process
the content of Office files protected by a label.

items.Requirement: Hide organisation-wide sharing claims from the people picker
items.Rationale: As long as the 'Everyone except external users', 'All Users' and 'Everyone' claims remain available in the SharePoint people picker, any site owner can make an entire library readable by the whole tenant in three clicks, with no malicious intent. Before Copilot that content was theoretically accessible but practically impossible to find; with Copilot a single natural language question surfaces it, including for a user who did not know the site existed. Hiding those claims at tenant level is the only preventive control that stops new internal oversharing from being created while the data access governance reports are used to clean up the existing stock: without it the organisation creates oversharing faster than it remediates, and the permission review never converges. This is what the Microsoft blueprint calls 'disable or restrict use of company-wide sharing groups' in the Guardrails pillar. The 'Everyone' and 'All Users' claims have no documented legitimate use: they cover guest accounts and external users already present in the directory. The EEEU claim may support a deliberate intranet scenario, in which case the exception must be documented and the sites concerned covered by Restricted Content Discovery or explicitly labelled as public. One caveat: the setting only affects new shares, it revokes no permission already granted.
items.Expected: ShowEveryoneExceptExternalUsersClaim = False, ShowAllUsersClaim = False and ShowEveryoneClaim = False. If the organisation keeps the EEEU claim for a legitimate intranet use case, the exception is documented and the sites concerned are covered by Restricted Content Discovery or accepted as public. The stock of shares already granted is handled separately, from the data access governance reports.
items.Verification: Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object ShowEveryoneExceptExternalUsersClaim, ShowAllUsersClaim, ShowEveryoneClaim ; Get-SPOSite -Limit All | Select-Object Url, DisableCompanyWideSharingLinks
items.HowTo:
1. Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com
2. Read the state of the three claims:
   Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object ShowEveryoneExceptExternalUsersClaim,
   ShowAllUsersClaim, ShowEveryoneClaim
3. Read the per-site complement:
   Get-SPOSite -Limit All | Select-Object Url, DisableCompanyWideSharingLinks
--- Remediation ---
4. Set-SPOTenant -ShowEveryoneClaim $false
5. Set-SPOTenant -ShowAllUsersClaim $false
6. Set-SPOTenant -ShowEveryoneExceptExternalUsersClaim $false
7. Disable 'People in your organization' links on sensitive sites:
   Set-SPOSite -Identity <url> -DisableCompanyWideSharingLinks Disabled
--- Clearing the existing stock ---
8. Open https://admin.cloud.microsoft > Admin centers > SharePoint
9. Left menu: Reports > Data access governance
10. Work through the 'Everyone except external users' report and remove
    the claim from the sites it lists
--- Note ---
The setting only affects NEW shares: it revokes no permission already granted.
SharePoint Administrator role required.

items.Requirement: Cover sensitive sites awaiting remediation with Restricted Content Discovery
items.Rationale: Restricted Content Discovery is the interim measure Microsoft now points to as the reference way of removing a site from Copilot answers and organisation-wide search while permissions are being reviewed. It is a per-site setting that changes no permission: the content stays accessible to those entitled to it, but it disappears from Copilot grounding and the site loses its AI entry points (Copilot button, AI actions, agent creation, create pages with AI). Without that cover, an HR, Finance or Executive site identified as overshared stays queryable in natural language by the whole tenant for the weeks or months it takes to fix the access control lists, which is exactly the window where the exposure is known and untreated. This requirement is the counterpart of requirement 21, which inventories restricted sites: it asks the opposite question, whether the high-risk sites reported by the data access governance reports are actually covered. The tenant allow-list mechanism (Restricted SharePoint Search, requirement 22) is not a substitute: it is capped at 100 sites, degrades search for every user and is being retired. Use must remain selective: applied broadly, the restriction removes legitimate content from Copilot and degrades answer relevance across the tenant. Finally, latency matters: on a site holding more than 500,000 items, indexing can take more than a week, which has to be anticipated before the go-live date.
items.Expected: Every site classified as high risk by the data access governance reports or by the content management assessment carries RestrictContentOrgWideSearch = True while its permissions are being fixed. No site that has not been identified as at risk is placed under restriction. DelegateRestrictedContentDiscoverabilityManagement = False, unless a documented governance decision says otherwise.
items.Verification: Get-SPOSite -Limit All | Select-Object Url, RestrictContentOrgWideSearch ; Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object DelegateRestrictedContentDiscoverabilityManagement ; Get-SPODataAccessGovernanceInsight -ReportEntity EveryoneExceptExternalUsersAtSite -Workload SharePoint
items.HowTo:
1. Open https://admin.cloud.microsoft > Admin centers > SharePoint
   (or https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com)
2. Left menu: Reports > Data access governance
3. Build the list of high-risk sites from the 'Everyone except external users'
   report and from the 'Permissioned users' report
--- Coverage, in PowerShell ---
4. Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com
5. Read the perimeter already covered:
   Get-SPOSite -Limit All | Select-Object Url, RestrictContentOrgWideSearch
6. Cover a site for the duration of the remediation:
   Set-SPOSite -Identity <url> -RestrictContentOrgWideSearch $true
7. Check that management is not delegated to site administrators:
   Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object DelegateRestrictedContentDiscoverabilityManagement
8. Take back control if needed:
   Set-SPOTenant -DelegateRestrictedContentDiscoverabilityManagement $false
--- Exiting the restriction ---
9. Once permissions are fixed:
   Set-SPOSite -Identity <url> -RestrictContentOrgWideSearch $false
--- Note ---
Restricted Content Discovery requires SharePoint Advanced Management and a
Microsoft 365 Copilot licence. Index propagation can take more than a week on a
site holding over 500,000 items: apply the cover well before the go-live date.
The engine never triggers Start-SPORestrictedContentDiscoverabilityReport.

items.Requirement: Rule explicitly on the scope of Copilot in SharePoint (KnowledgeAgentScope)
items.Rationale: Copilot in SharePoint, formerly AI in SharePoint, ships as an opt-out preview: no administrator action is required to receive it, it simply becomes available to licensed users. In practice, a natural language questioning capability appears on sites the organisation has not audited yet, at the exact moment when oversharing remediation is usually still under way. The only control point is PowerShell: the KnowledgeAgentScope parameter of Set-SPOTenant, whose values are AllSites, IncludeSelectedSites, ExcludeSelectedSites and NoSites, together with the KnowledgeAgentSelectedSitesList capped at 100 sites. There is no equivalent user interface. Without an explicit, recorded decision the organisation inherits the service default instead of choosing it, and the security committee discovers the feature after the fact, often through an incident. The requirement does not audit the preview capability itself but the setting that exposes the tenant to it: that is a governance decision, it can be challenged, and it must precede go-live. Field note: the parameter requires SharePoint Online Management Shell 16.0.26615.12013 or later, otherwise the command fails with 'A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name KnowledgeAgentScope', and the setting must be replayed for each geography in a Multi-Geo tenant.
items.Expected: KnowledgeAgentScope carries an explicitly decided and documented value: NoSites or IncludeSelectedSites while the oversharing audit is unfinished, AllSites only after remediation. KnowledgeAgentSelectedSitesList is consistent with the decision and stays under the 100-site cap. In a Multi-Geo tenant the decision is applied to every geography.
items.Verification: Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object KnowledgeAgentScope, KnowledgeAgentSelectedSitesList
items.HowTo:
1. Check the module version:
   Get-Module Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell -ListAvailable | Select-Object Version
   (16.0.26615.12013 minimum)
2. Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com
3. Read the scope in force:
   Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object KnowledgeAgentScope, KnowledgeAgentSelectedSitesList
--- Decision ---
4. Suspend the capability while the oversharing audit runs:
   Set-SPOTenant -KnowledgeAgentScope NoSites
5. Or limit it to a pilot perimeter:
   Set-SPOTenant -KnowledgeAgentScope IncludeSelectedSites
   Set-SPOTenant -KnowledgeAgentSelectedSitesList <url1>,<url2>
6. Or open it after remediation:
   Set-SPOTenant -KnowledgeAgentScope AllSites
7. Record the decision in the AI governance register
--- Multi-Geo ---
8. Replay steps 2 to 6 against each geo admin centre
--- Note ---
There is NO user interface for this parameter.
The scope list is capped at 100 sites.
SharePoint Administrator role required.

items.Requirement: Inventory the agents created in SharePoint and the sites that concentrate them
items.Rationale: Agents created in SharePoint are .agent files stored in each site's assets library: their governance goes through neither the Microsoft 365 app catalogue, nor Copilot Studio, nor the agent settings of the admin centre. They therefore fall entirely outside the requirements of this baseline that cover agents and extensions, which makes them a complete blind spot. A user who creates an agent on an overshared site produces a conversational entry point into all of that site's content, available to anyone who can reach the site, and blocking an agent from the Microsoft 365 admin centre currently applies to Copilot Chat only, neither to SharePoint nor to OneDrive. Microsoft now provides a dedicated report through SharePoint Online PowerShell, with three contents: agents per site, top 100 sites, and distribution. It makes sprawl measurable and lets the sites concerned be cross-checked against the list of sensitive or overshared sites. Without that inventory, the organisation does not know how many agents exist, on which sites they were created, or whether one of them opens a conversation over a site the permission review has just flagged. The report is triggered and read later: the audit engine only reads pre-existing reports and triggers a generation solely on explicit operator request, so as to remain free of side effects.
items.Expected: A SharePoint agent inventory report exists, with status Completed and dated less than 90 days ago. No agent is created on a site identified as sensitive (HR, Finance, Executive, Legal) or on a site with high external sharing, and sites covered by Restricted Content Discovery expose no agent. The per-site detail is downloaded and worked through, not merely generated.

items.Requirement: Verify that Microsoft Loop and Microsoft Whiteboard are enabled on the tenant
items.Rationale: The official Copilot requirements page lists Microsoft Loop and Microsoft Whiteboard among the applications to enable at tenant level, and none of the historical requirements in this baseline covered them. Without Loop enabled, Copilot in Loop is unavailable and Copilot Pages are only interactive inside the Copilot app: they cannot be shared as components in Teams, Outlook, OneNote or Whiteboard, which removes the main mechanism for collaborating around Copilot answers. Without Whiteboard enabled, Copilot in Whiteboard is unavailable. Both switches are frequently still False on tenants deployed before 2023, or were turned off deliberately to limit the sprawl of SharePoint Embedded containers, a decision rarely revisited when Copilot is rolled out. In practice, two Copilot surfaces that are bought and billed are never reachable, and users following official Copilot training find that part of the demonstrations does not work for them, which weighs directly on adoption. The tenant switch is not sufficient on its own: the Cloud Policy setting 'Create and view Loop files in Microsoft apps that support Loop' and the Loop entry under Org settings must be consistent with it. Turning the surfaces off remains a legitimate governance decision, provided it is documented and those surfaces are removed from the training programme.

items.Requirement: Deploy DSPM for AI: default policies and detection of risky AI usage
items.Rationale: Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) for AI is the Purview entry point dedicated to governing Copilot, agents and third-party AI: data risk assessments, an activity explorer over AI interaction events, and above all a set of default policies deployable in one click. Every other requirement in this checklist looks at configuration; this one is the only one that looks at abnormal usage, that is to say prompt injection, mass access from a compromised account, or the departing employee querying Copilot about the customer file. Four policy families cover blind spots no other control sees: 'Detect risky AI usage' on the Insider Risk Management side, 'Unethical behavior in AI apps' on the communication compliance side, 'Capture interactions for Copilot experiences' to make interactions defensible in eDiscovery, and 'Protect sensitive data from Copilot processing' on the DLP side. Because the service normalises their names, their presence can be verified by script, which turns an intention into a finding. Without them the organisation has no unified AI posture dashboard and discovers after the fact how much oversharing Copilot is exploiting, usually during an incident. A policy that is deployed but left as a draft or in simulation produces neither alert nor evidence: it gives false assurance and is therefore reported separately. The state of the solution itself, its risk assessments and its recommendations, has no public API and remains a portal observation. The requirement leaves the score when the tenant holds neither Insider Risk Management nor communication compliance, since the default policies cannot exist in that case.
items.Expected: At least three DSPM for AI default policies created and active, covering as a minimum the families 'DSPM for AI - Detect risky AI usage' (Insider Risk Management), 'DSPM for AI - Unethical behavior in AI apps' (communication compliance) and 'DSPM for AI - Capture interactions for Copilot experiences' (collection policy). The 'DSPM for AI - Protect sensitive data from Copilot processing' policy completes the setup on the DLP side. Associated prerequisites: Purview auditing turned on, Copilot licences assigned, devices onboarded and the Purview browser extension deployed if third-party AI must be covered. At least one data risk assessment run before opening licences beyond the pilot (a portal observation, no API). A policy that is present but inactive, draft or in simulation does not count as coverage.

2. Check the prerequisites: Settings > Audit (logging turned on), Copilot licences assigned, devices onboarded to Microsoft Purview if third-party AI must be covered
3. Left-hand menu: Solutions > Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) for AI
4. Overview > Recommendations: deploy the suggested default policies, in particular 'DSPM for AI - Detect risky AI usage', 'DSPM for AI - Unethical behavior in AI apps' and 'DSPM for AI - Capture interactions for Copilot experiences'
5. For every deployed policy: check that it is turned on and not left as a draft or in simulation
6. Data risk assessments: run the default assessment on SharePoint sites and OneDrive accounts, then act on the oversharing recommendations
7. Reports: track AI interactions and the sensitive information types referenced in prompts and responses

items.Requirement: Copilot connectivity: required endpoints reachable, WebSocket (WSS) allowed and no TLS inspection
items.Rationale: The checklist carried no network requirement at all, even though the official Copilot prerequisites page devotes a whole section to the subject and this is the hardest failure mode to diagnose. Several Copilot integrations rely on WebSocket (WSS) connections towards *.cloud.microsoft and *.office.com: a network perimeter that blocks the WSS protocol, an appliance that decrypts and re-signs TLS traffic, or a proxy that enforces aggressive session lifetimes all cause Copilot application failures while every other tenant check stays green. The *.cloud.microsoft domain is a required endpoint (entry id=184, Default category, required=true) of the Microsoft 365 endpoints service, and Microsoft is progressively consolidating the Copilot experiences under it. For Copilot Cowork, the documentation additionally forbids TLS inspection of *.gateway.prod.island.powerapps.com and any absolute session lifetime below 30 minutes on long-lived flows. Concrete consequence when the requirement is not met: Copilot opens and then fails with no usable error message, support concludes it is a licensing or policy defect, and the organisation spends weeks auditing an already compliant tenant while the real blockage sits on a network appliance nobody thought to question. TLS re-signing is the costliest case: Microsoft does not support it for Copilot traffic, and it produces intermittent errors that the workstation logs nowhere. This check is the only one in the checklist that explains the 'everything is green in the tenant and Copilot still does not work' case. Its evidence scope is however limited to the reference workstation it runs on and to the network path that workstation takes: it does not stand for the whole fleet.
items.HowTo:
1. Work from a reference workstation of the fleet, behind the same proxy and the same inspection appliance as the users
2. Open https://endpoints.office.com/endpoints/worldwide?clientrequestid=<GUID> in the browser and note entry id=184 (urls = *.cloud.microsoft, category = Default, required = true, tcpPorts = 443)

4. Open https://m365.cloud.microsoft in Microsoft Edge, click the padlock icon in the address bar, then 'Connection is secure' > 'Certificate is valid', and read the 'Issued by' field
